title: The '90s Queen Just Did the Bravest Thing of Her Career. Karisma Kapoor Is Unrecognisable in Brown.
excerpt: No glamour, no gloss — just an alcoholic Kolkata cop with a body to find and a past she can't outrun. Karisma's neo-noir comeback is the boldest swing of her digital life.
body:
For three decades, the camera loved **Karisma Kapoor** a certain way: luminous, dancing, the dimpled queen of *Raja Hindustani* who could make an entire generation fall in love between two beats of a song. So the first shock of **Brown** is simply seeing her stripped of all of it. No glow. No gloss. Just a woman rolling her own smokes, shoulders heavy with exhaustion, hunting a killer through a Kolkata that never stops raining.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=prdjv5IWPWY</youtube>

This is **DCP Rita Brown** — an Anglo-Indian detective with the Kolkata Police, an alcoholic carrying "a lot of unresolved trauma," and the most uncomfortable, fully-inhabited role Karisma has ever taken. Streaming now on **ZEE5**, the seven-episode neo-noir is the kind of swing that could have gone badly wrong. It didn't.

## The plunge


![Raja Hindustani — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/e/ea/Raja_Hindustani_poster.jpg)



> **"I am really happy that Lolo actually took the plunge." — Kareena Kapoor Khan

That word — *plunge* — is exactly right."**



When the special screening happened, the family showed up — and so did the headline. **Kareena Kapoor Khan** and **Saif Ali Khan** arrived to cheer on Lolo, and Kareena said the thing everyone was thinking.

> "It is so nice to finally see Lolo, the absolute '90s queen, back on screen. People try to do roles in their comfort zone, but Karisma has always tried to do things differently — be it Fizaa or Zubeidaa. I am really happy that Lolo actually took the plunge." — Kareena Kapoor Khan

That word — *plunge* — is exactly right. Brown isn't a polite return to acting. It's a freefall into pitch-black material. Writer **Mayukh Ghosh**, of the acclaimed *Hostages*, says Rita was "always intended to contrast with a glamorous lead," and that Karisma began her preparation not with the emotion but with the body. "There's a tangible physicality to her character," Ghosh said, "reflected in her movements and the weight of her exhaustion." You feel it in every frame — the slump, the tremor, the way she looks at a corpse like she's already seen too many.

## A thriller that refuses to be binged


![Rita Brown — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/82/Portrait_of_Rita_Mae_Brown.jpg)


Directed by **Abhinay Deo** — the man who gave us the anarchic *Delhi Belly* — Brown is a different animal entirely: hard-boiled, morally fractured, drenched in monsoon dread. Based on **Abheek Barua**'s 2016 novel *City of Death*, it opens with the murder of a teenage girl from a prominent family and spirals into the hunt for a serial killer targeting women across Kolkata's class divides. Gaurav Chatterji's score broods. Amogh Deshpande's camera treats the city like a wound.

The ensemble around Karisma is quietly stacked — **Surya Sharma** as her grieving junior partner, **Jisshu Sengupta**, **Soni Razdan**, the legendary **Helen**, and **Ajinkya Deo**. In an interview this week, Soni Razdan offered a piece of advice that doubles as the show's mission statement: this is not a thriller to inhale in one sitting. Brown wants to be sat with, episode by episode, the way the best noir demands you marinate in its gloom.

There's pedigree here too. Back in 2023, Brown became the **first Indian web series ever selected for Berlinale Series Market Selects** — Berlin's showcase of standout global series. That's not a marketing line; it's a signal that this was always meant to be more than a star vehicle.

## Where the diaspora can watch

For NRIs, the good news is simple: Brown is streaming on **ZEE5 Global**, which carries the platform's originals across the US, UK, Canada, and beyond. The series even wears its diaspora audience on its sleeve — its promotional push leaned hard into the Indians-in-London, Indians-in-the-UK crowd, the very viewers who've kept Karisma's '90s filmography alive on living-room rewatches for thirty years.

And that's the real story underneath the murder mystery. Brown is a film-star's reinvention staged for a streaming age — a reminder that the actresses who defined the '90s aren't relics to be nostalgically replayed, but artists still willing to risk everything for a role that scares them. Karisma Kapoor could have spent the rest of her career being adored. Instead she chose to be unrecognisable. That's not a comeback. That's a statement.
